\title{DSA4213 Assignment 1: Do Better Next-Word Predictors\\
Give Better Sentiment Features, and at What Cost?}

\author{Lee Kai Rong, Student ID: A0287723U \\
  Code Repo: \url{https://github.com/kr7001/dsa4213-assignment}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Do language models that predict the next word better also give better sentiment features, and what does the better prediction cost? On \href{https://amazon-reviews-2023.github.io/}{Amazon beauty reviews}, a Kneser-Ney 5-gram and an RNN, LSTM and Transformer of equal core size (0.37M parameters) reach test perplexity 60.9, 50.1, 40.8 and 41.2; the neural models train for 25 to 30 minutes, the 5-gram for 14 seconds. Fixing the LSTM's input word vectors instead of learning them raises its perplexity by 11\% with my own skip-gram vectors and by 29\% with GloVe, despite GloVe's 1,100 times larger corpus. I then freeze 19 networks and train a linear classifier on the 100-number vector just before each network's output layer, taken after a review's last word or averaged over all words. Across the 13 distinct models (78 pairs), the better next-word predictor is also the better classifier in 66 pairs with last-word vectors (Kendall's $\tau = 0.69$) and in 72 with averaged ones ($\tau = 0.85$). The RNN is the main exception: its last-word vectors score 4 points below its averaged ones, consistent with its short memory in \hyperref[sec:part1]{Part~I}, where its lead over the 5-gram stops growing after about five tokens. The best features (93.4\% accuracy) match, but do not beat, tf-idf counts of words and word pairs (93.6\%), which need no language model.
\end{abstract}

%=====================================================================
\section{Question and Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

One question runs through all three parts: \emph{does a language model that predicts the next word better also give better features for sentiment classification, and what does the better prediction cost?} The answer is open: GPT-1's zero-shot sentiment accuracy rose steadily with pre-training \citep[Sec.~5]{radford2018improving}, but models with equal pre-training loss can differ downstream \citep{liu2023same}. Part~I compares model designs and their costs, Part~II input word vectors; together they train 19 neural language models whose test cross-entropy $J$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:j}; lower is better) ranges from 3.57 nats (best) to 4.03 (worst), a spread wide enough to test the question. Part~III freezes all 19 and tests, with one linear classifier, whether lower $J$ gives higher sentiment accuracy. Every setting was fixed before the results it affects, from a measurement on this data or published evidence, with three exceptions (Appendix~\ref{app:decisions}; each decision's rejected alternatives and evidence: Tables~\ref{tab:decisions-a} and~\ref{tab:decisions-b}). Results paragraphs give observations first, then \textbf{possible explanations}. Code, seeds and AI use: Appendix~\ref{app:repro}.

\paragraph{Corpus.}
I chose the All\_Beauty reviews of Amazon Reviews 2023 \citep{hou2024bridging} over six other corpora (comparison: Table~\ref{tab:corpora}) for three reasons: (1)~star ratings give in-domain sentiment labels for Part~III; (2)~all reviews of a product can be kept on one side of every split, so no test product reaches language-model training; (3)~reviews are unlikely to be in GloVe's Wikipedia and Gigaword text, so Part~II tests GloVe on text it has not seen. Text is lowercased, numbers become \tok{num} (so prices and sizes need no vocabulary entries), and the course tokenizer \citep{zhou2026notebooks} keeps words, contractions and six punctuation marks.

\paragraph{Filters.}
From 701,528 raw reviews, four filters remove, each with a threshold measured on this data (counts: Table~\ref{tab:data}): (i)~empty reviews and reviews over 512 tokens, so one Transformer context holds any review; short reviews stay, as a 3-word minimum would remove 8.7\% of positive but only 3.4\% of negative reviews and skew Part~III's labels (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}a); (ii)~non-English reviews, as the brief asks for English: the usual detector fastText is unreliable on very short reviews (in a sample of 25 one- or two-word reviews it judged non-English with under 50\% confidence, only 11 were), so reviews of up to six words are judged by my own word score, which measures how much more common their words are in non-English reviews (Tables~\ref{tab:language} and~\ref{tab:handchecks}); (iii)~a person's repeated reviews and identical reviews of 14+ words by different people, as shorter matches such as ``love it'' are everyday phrases (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}b); (iv)~reviews beyond 90 per product, so popular products cannot dominate (the top 1\% held 28\% of reviews); as reviews of one product are alike, 90 keep 95\% of what they tell about its rating \citep[Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}c;][]{kish1965survey}. 587,133 reviews (21.2M tokens) remain (checks: Table~\ref{tab:checks}).

\paragraph{Splits and vocabulary.}
To prevent leakage, I split by product, not by review: each product gets a random key (seed 4213) that sends all its reviews to one of five piles: language-model training (50\% of products; 10.96M targets), validation (5\%; 1.07M), test (5\%; 1.12M), Part~III test (10\%) and Part~III training (30\%). So no evaluation or Part~III product is seen in language-model training, and 5\% is enough for validation and test: it measures $J$ to within about 0.003 nats (one standard error), far below the gaps compared here (sizes: Appendix~\ref{app:data}). The vocabulary is every token seen 5+ times in language-model training, plus \tok{pad} (batching), \tok{unk} (unseen tokens), \tok{bos} and \tok{eos} (review start and end), $|V| = 17{,}068$. A cut-off of 5 leaves only 0.60\% of test targets as \tok{unk}, so a lower one would add thousands of words too rare to learn while removing few unknowns (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}d); 5 is also gensim's default, so Part~II's skip-gram sees every word at least five times.

\paragraph{Scoring.}
All models face the same prediction problem \citep[slide~29]{zhou2026lecture3}: each review is scored on its own from $x_1 = \tok{bos}$, so no model uses another person's review as context; review $r$ has $T_r$ targets (its tokens and \tok{eos}), $N = \sum_r T_r$, and
\begin{equation}
\Jtest = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{r}\sum_{t=1}^{T_r} -\log P_\theta\big(x^{(r)}_{t+1} \,\big|\, x^{(r)}_{1:t}\big),
\label{eq:j}
\end{equation}
with $\mathrm{PPL} = \exp(\Jtest)$. $J$ is in nats (natural-log units); 0.1 nats less is about 10\% lower perplexity. Padding is masked, and the code asserts the same $N$ for every model (1,115,210 test targets).

%=====================================================================
\section{Part I: Four Language Models}
\label{sec:part1}

\paragraph{Models.}
The $n$-gram baseline is my own interpolated modified Kneser-Ney 5-gram, the best smoothing in \citeauthor{chen1998empirical}'s \citeyearpar{chen1998empirical} comparison, with the course's add-$k$ 5-gram \citep{zhou2026notebooks} as a second baseline; validation picks their settings. Each neural design has two sizes: S (main) and M, with about 4 times the core parameters, to check whether the ranking of designs survives a change of size. The RNN \citep{elman1990finding} and LSTM \citep{hochreiter1997long} have one recurrent layer (S: 512 and 248 units) and carry $h^{(t)}$ (and $c^{(t)}$) through the whole review; the Transformer (S: three causal pre-LN layers, $d_{\text{model}} = 100$, 4 heads) sees up to 513 tokens, which holds every review, so each model uses its natural context. To compare designs, not sizes, all three have the same word tables (input table $E$, $|V| \times 100$, and an untied output layer; 3.4M parameters) and cores, everything else, within 2.3\% of each other in size \citep{kaplan2020scaling,collins2017capacity}; the unit counts are set to meet that budget (Table~\ref{tab:pilot}), since equal hidden units would give unequal sizes. $d_{\text{model}} = 100$ matches Part~II's GloVe vectors; pre-LN \citep{xiong2020layer} with sinusoidal positions needs no long warm-up or position parameters (Table~\ref{tab:decisions-a}).

\paragraph{Training.}
The three networks share training settings, each chosen from evidence before any result (source for each: Table~\ref{tab:recipe}): AdamW (weight decay 0.1); batches of 8,192 token positions, beyond which five of six models stopped training faster in a pilot run (Figure~\ref{fig:batch}); a 4\% warm-up, then cosine decay over 6 epochs, the longest budget that let all tuning tries finish overnight; clipping at 1.0; and validation $J$ 4 times per epoch, keeping the best checkpoint. Dropout is 0: with 0.35 parameters per training target (AWD-LSTM: 16 to 26; \citealp{merity2018regularizing}), overfitting was unlikely, and a rule written before training would have added dropout to all three if any model overfitted before the last quarter of its run (rules: Appendix~\ref{app:rules}). Only the peak learning rate is tuned, by one search for all models with every try a full run, since the winner can depend on the tuning budget \citep{dodge2019show} (every try: Table~\ref{tab:tuning}).

\paragraph{Prediction quality.}
On test cross-entropy $J$, every S model beats the 5-gram: the LSTM and Transformer by about 0.4 nats (perplexity about 41 against 61), the RNN by 0.20 (Table~\ref{tab:part1}). The LSTM and Transformer are only 0.010 nats apart, about 2.6 standard deviations of seed noise (estimated from only three LSTM-S seeds; Section~\ref{sec:part2}), so with one run each I do not rank them firmly; at M the Transformer leads by a clearer 0.032, and the RNN gets worse with size. $J$ by position for the S models (Figure~\ref{fig:positions}, Table~\ref{tab:positions}) shows where the neural models gain: on the first 4 targets, where the 5-gram sees the whole history, they lead it by only 0.04 to 0.10 nats, so little of their edge comes from better word statistics; from target 5, where the 5-gram's window starts to drop words, the lead jumps to 0.22 (RNN) and 0.38 (LSTM, Transformer), so it comes from longer context; and only the LSTM's and Transformer's lead keeps growing, so only they use distant context. At S the Transformer is better on targets 1 to 8 and the LSTM from target 33; the LSTM's whole 0.010 lead comes from targets beyond 64 (22\% of the test set), so the better design depends on review length.
\hyp The RNN's flat lead fits vanishing gradients \citep{bengio1994learning}, which clipping cannot fix. The small Transformer may trail on long reviews because few positions lie that far in (8\% of targets are beyond 128) and its 100-number states leave little room; the deficit disappears at size M, as a capacity limit would predict (untested). RNN-M is worse than RNN-S although 4 times larger, and its gradients were clipped in 30\% of steps (RNN-S 12\%), which suggests it is harder to optimise rather than short of capacity.

\paragraph{Cost and trade-offs.}
Per prediction, the three S designs cost almost the same (Table~\ref{tab:part1}): arithmetic within 2\%, most of it in the shared output layer, and similar scoring speed. Their real difference is training: Transformer-S trains for 29.7 minutes against 24.7 (LSTM-S) and 25.1 (RNN-S), and tuning took 1.7 to 2.6 hours per model. The 5-gram is the opposite trade-off: it counts in 14 seconds and scores 75 to 80 times faster on the CPU, but needs a 425~MB table and predicts 0.2 to 0.4 nats worse. Size M costs 1.5 to 1.6 times the arithmetic and 17 to 28\% more training time, and pays off only for the LSTM and Transformer.

\paragraph{Learning behaviour.}
For every model, validation $J$ still falls at the end of 6 epochs, above the training sample (Figure~\ref{fig:curves}a), and every best checkpoint is one of the last two of 25 checks: no model overfits, so the dropout rule never fired. Were 6 epochs enough? The last epoch still gained 0.013 to 0.025 nats, more than the LSTM-Transformer gap, so a second rule written in advance gave all three 10-epoch runs (Figure~\ref{fig:curves-appendix}): the ranking held (LSTM ahead by 0.016), and only the Transformer stopped early, at 9.7 epochs, on its first sign of overfitting (validation $J$ stalled while training $J$ fell), too late to trigger the dropout rule.
\hyp The Transformer fits its training text most closely (after 6 epochs its training sample sits 0.190 nats below validation, against 0.140 and 0.105), so without dropout it overfits first.

\paragraph{Generated text.}
I sample with temperature, $q_{t,T}(w) \propto p_t(w)^{1/T}$ \citep[slide~21]{zhou2026lecture3}, one $T$ for all models so the comparison is matched. Rather than adopt the course's $T = 0.8$, I measured it: on 300 validation openings, $T = 1.01$ makes each Part~I model's own text about as surprising to it as real text (Figure~\ref{fig:curves}c), the calibration check of \citet[Sec.~4.2]{holtzman2020curious}; at $T = 0.8$ the text would be 1.1 to 1.5 nats too predictable and repeat 4-grams up to 3.9\% of the time. Each sample is 22 new tokens, a median review's length; for six prompts fixed before generation, every model writes 9 samples and I show the middle one by its own perplexity, so the shown sample is typical, not hand-picked. Over 300 test openings, neural text repeats 4-grams slightly more than real text and varies slightly less, while the 5-gram varies most and copies the most training 5-grams (all measures: Table~\ref{tab:generation}). In the samples (all six prompts: Table~\ref{tab:samples-all}), the 5-gram is fluent over a few words but drifts (``disappointed \ldots a fuller, healthier''), the LSTM keeps prompt~3's complaint going (``felt greasy \ldots didn't even care for''), the Transformer keeps prompt~6's daughter as the subject (``she loves this product''), and every model breaks grammar within 22 tokens (``vibrant black black hair'').
\hyp The 5-gram sees only four previous tokens, so its text is locally plausible but globally loose, and it generates from counts, so it copies most. Low copying by the neural models is not creativity, since broken word combinations are new too.

\paragraph{Part~I in brief.}
At equal size the LSTM and Transformer predict best (tied at S, the Transformer ahead at M), the RNN uses little distant context, and the 5-gram is cheapest but weakest. Part~II uses the LSTM-S (lowest validation $J$, a rule fixed in advance); Part~III asks whether these differences carry over to sentiment.

%=====================================================================
\section{Part II: Embedding Variants}
\label{sec:part2}

\paragraph{Design.}
Part~II varies only the LSTM-S's input table, at $d = 100$: GloVe's 300 dimensions improve its analogies but add little as model input (CoNLL-03 F1 90.34 against 90.72; \citealp{carlson2025new}) and would triple the table (reasons: Table~\ref{tab:decisions-b}). Three settings: (1)~a random table trained with the model (Part~I's LSTM-S); (2)~my skip-gram vectors \citep[Lecture~2 settings;][]{mikolov2013distributed}, trained on the training pile, then frozen; (3)~GloVe 2024 (Wikipedia and Gigaword, 11.9B tokens; newer words than GloVe 2014), frozen. GloVe differs from the random table in two ways, extra data and freezing, so two extra runs separate them: GloVe left trainable (extra data, no freezing) and a frozen random table at GloVe's scale (freezing, no information). My table is scaled to GloVe's root mean square, as with Adam a fixed input's scale acts like a learning rate for the first layer. The three settings run with three seeds each (the extra runs with one) from the same starting weights and batches at the Part~I learning rate (0.01); fingerprints confirm frozen tables never change. GloVe covers 97.0\% of the vocabulary once contractions and tokenizer splits are built from their pieces; the rest get random vectors with GloVe's variance \citep{kim2014convolutional} (coverage: Appendix~\ref{app:part2}). My vectors took 9.7 minutes on one CPU thread, against about 24 per LSTM run.

\caption{Part~II (LSTM-S). \textit{Test J:} mean and SD over three seeds (one in the last two rows). \textit{Valid J:} after epochs 1 and 6. \textit{V$-$T:} validation minus training-sample $J$ at the best checkpoint (higher: more overfitting).}

\paragraph{Results.}
Freezing hurts on every seed (Appendix~\ref{app:part2}), on average by 0.100 nats with my vectors and 0.257 with GloVe (Table~\ref{tab:part2}): frozen in-domain vectors beat GloVe despite its 1,100 times larger corpus. The extra runs (seed 4213) show why. Freezing a table with no word information at GloVe's scale costs 0.319 nats (freezing plus a larger scale; Appendix~\ref{app:part2}); at that same scale, my vectors win back 0.215 of it but GloVe only 0.053, so GloVe's knowledge helps little when frozen. Trainable GloVe starts ahead, is level after one epoch and ends 0.021 nats behind (Table~\ref{tab:part2}), so its extra data buys only a head start. \emph{Convergence:} frozen tables end higher rather than learn more slowly (Figure~\ref{fig:curves}b); my vectors even lead at the first check on every seed. \emph{Stability:} frozen settings vary more across seeds but overfit less (Table~\ref{tab:part2}), with similar gradient norms, and the order holds at each setting's best learning rate (Appendix~\ref{app:part2}). \emph{Generated text:} frozen tables copy fewer training 5-grams and vary more (Table~\ref{tab:generation}), with breakdowns such as ``i don't not stop my hair'' (GloVe, frozen; Table~\ref{tab:samples-all}).
\hyp Trainability matters most: 10.7M review tokens suffice to learn the table. GloVe knows more about words in general (WordSim353 0.52 against 0.39; analogies 57.5\% against 22.1\%; Table~\ref{tab:part2-words}), yet frozen it helps less than my vectors, plausibly (untested) because of word sense: my neighbours of ``cheap'' include \emph{cheaply, flimsy, crappy}, GloVe's \emph{inexpensive, cheaper, affordable}, and reviews need the complaint sense. The shared $T$ acts hotter for frozen tables (own-text minus real-text $J$: +0.19 to +0.29), which may explain their less coherent samples.

\paragraph{Part~II in brief.}
Learning the table beats freezing it, and frozen in-domain vectors beat a far larger general corpus; Part~III ranks these models too.

%=====================================================================
\section{Part III: Downstream Representations}
\label{sec:part3}

\paragraph{Setup.}
Reviews with 1 to 2 stars are negative and 4 to 5 positive; 3-star reviews are left out as ambiguous, and classes are balanced so accuracy is meaningful (74,344 training and 24,362 test reviews, from products no language model saw). Each review passes through a frozen model after \tok{bos}, and I take the 100 numbers that feed its output layer, the same size in every model, so no model wins by a longer vector (top hidden states give close results: Table~\ref{tab:part3-all}). Two readouts make one vector per review: the state after its last token (word or punctuation; ``last word'' below), which the model uses to predict what comes next, and the average of the states after every token (never \tok{bos} or padding). All 19 models enter, in groups that change one factor (design, size, training length, word table, seed). References show what the features add: untrained copies of the S designs (does training matter? \citealp{wieting2019no}), averaged word tables (do states add to word vectors?), tf-idf counts of words and word pairs (a strong classic baseline; \citealp{wang2012baselines}) and review length. Every representation gets the same L2 logistic regression \citep{pedregosa2011scikit} on standardised features, a linear probe, since a stronger classifier could learn the task itself and hide differences \citep{hewitt2019designing}. Its regularisation strength $C$ comes from 5-fold cross-validation on training reviews, folds split by product as the test set is, and the test set is used once (details: Appendix~\ref{app:part3}). I report accuracy with 95\% bootstrap intervals ($\pm$0.3 to 0.5 points), test 51 comparisons fixed in advance with exact McNemar tests \citep{dietterich1998approximate}, Holm-corrected \citep{holm1979simple}, and measure ranking agreement over the 13 seed-4213 models with Kendall's $\tau$: the share of the 78 model pairs in the same order by test $J$ and accuracy, minus the share in the opposite order (1: same order).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{part3.pdf}
\caption{Sentiment accuracy against test $J$ for the 13 seed-4213 models, read at the last word (a) or averaged (b). Diamonds: Part~II's word tables, all on LSTM-S. Untrained copies (61 to 73\%) and length alone (52\%) lie below the plots (every accuracy: Table~\ref{tab:part3}).}
\label{fig:part3}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Results.}
(1)~Better next-word prediction goes with better features (Figure~\ref{fig:part3}): the rankings agree on 66 of 78 pairs at the last word ($\tau = 0.69$, nominal $p = 0.0005$) and 72 of 78 averaged ($\tau = 0.85$, $p < 10^{-5}$). This holds within single factors, design (3 of 3 pairs) and word table (9 and 10 of 10), and without reviews under 3 or 5 words, so neither one group nor very short reviews drive it. (2)~Language-model training makes the features: untrained copies reach only 61 to 73\%, and training adds 24 to 29 points at the last word. (3)~The readout matters most for the RNN: its last-word state loses 4.4 (S) and 4.1 (M) points against its average, while the LSTM's and Transformer's readouts differ by at most 0.74. On reviews over 20 words RNN-S falls to 79.9\% at the last word against 87.0\% averaged (Figure~\ref{fig:part3-length}). Five of the 12 out-of-order pairs involve an RNN; the other seven differ by at most 0.6 points, within seed noise (seed SD 0.31 points; Table~\ref{tab:part3}). (4)~Size, training length and word table mostly move accuracy the same way as $J$; for example, frozen GloVe loses 2.9 points to the trainable table at the last word and my frozen vectors only 0.3, the same order as in Part~II (36 of the 51 fixed comparisons significant after correction: Table~\ref{tab:comparisons}). (5)~The best features, LSTM-M and Transformer-M at the last word (93.4\% and 93.3\%; all accuracies: Table~\ref{tab:part3}), match but do not beat tf-idf counts (93.6\%; exploratory McNemar $p = 0.29$ and 0.07), which need no language model but 153,041 features instead of 100.
\hyp To predict a review's next words a model must track the writer's opinion, so a better predictor may store more sentiment in its state; this is a consistent correlation across groups that change one factor, not a causal test. The RNN's last state may keep little of a long review's start (Part~I); averaging keeps every position.

\paragraph{Errors.}
To see where the best predictor (Transformer-M, last word) fails, I compare groups defined before reading any error (Table~\ref{tab:errors}): reviews with a contrast word such as ``but'' (25\% of the test set) fall to 87.6\% from 95.2\%, 4-star reviews to 78.6\%, while negation costs little; word counts fail in the same groups, so these reviews are hard for both. Yet the two err on different reviews: each is right on about 850 that the other gets wrong, and at least one is right on 97.0\%, so they are complementary. To avoid hand-picked examples, I categorised 40 random mistakes (counts: Table~\ref{tab:error-categories}): the largest group (17) weigh real good and bad points; others state a complaint as plain fact (``leaves a greasy residue.''), praise through ``not'' (``a light scent. not overpowering''), or dismiss their one good point (``the packaging was nice but that's the only plus'').
\hyp In my reading, most remaining errors would puzzle a human too: mixed reviews rated by how the writer weighs the points, and 4-star reviews that list complaints.

%=====================================================================
\section{Synthesis, Limitations and Lessons}
\label{sec:synthesis}

\paragraph{The answer.}
Mostly yes: across design, size, training length and word table, the better next-word predictor gives better sentiment features in 85 to 92\% of model pairs, and in every pair at least 0.05 nats apart once features are averaged (exploratory; Table~\ref{tab:exploratory}). The main exception links Parts~I and~III: the RNN, whose lead over the 5-gram stops growing after about five tokens, scores 7 points lower at its last word than averaged on reviews over 20 words. Part~II's ranking also carries over: trainability beats 1,100 times more general text. The better prediction costs 17 to 22\% more training time and 1.5 to 1.6 times the arithmetic (LSTM-M, Transformer-M), and buys features that match word counts with 100 numbers learnt without labels.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Each Part~I model has one seed, so close gaps (LSTM-S and Transformer-S) stay unranked; all models are small and see one domain. The 13 ranked models share data and designs, so the $J$-accuracy link is a consistent correlation, not a causal test. A linear probe shows what frozen features hold, not what fine-tuning would reach. Preprocessing limits are measured in Table~\ref{tab:limits}.

\paragraph{Future work.}
Next I would add seeds and sizes, shuffle distant words to test the RNN's context, and combine counts with model features, which err on different reviews (at least one is right on 97.0\%).

\paragraph{Lessons learnt.}
(1)~\emph{Measure, don't borrow:} the course's $T = 0.8$ would have made every model's text 1.1 to 1.5 nats too predictable, so I measured $T$ on this data, as I did for the filters and the vocabulary cut-off. (2)~\emph{Fix the rules before the results:} the product split, equal core sizes, one tuning search and rules written in advance (Appendix~\ref{app:rules}) kept the comparisons fair; a rule, not my judgement, chose 10 epochs. (3)~\emph{Look inside averages:} one $J$ hid the LSTM's and Transformer's different strengths, one accuracy hid that word counts and the best model fail on different reviews, and the last-word readout made the RNN look weaker than its averaged states are. (4)~\emph{Relevant data beats more data:} when frozen, my vectors from 10.7M review tokens beat GloVe's from 1,100 times more text, plausibly because they learn the reviewers' sense of words such as ``cheap''. (5)~\emph{Keep a simple baseline:} word counts matched the best features and kept my claims about pre-training honest. (6)~\emph{Automate the evidence:} scripts write every table and check every number in the text against the results, so revisions stay consistent.

\section{Data and Preprocessing Evidence}
\label{app:data}

\paragraph{Choice of corpus.}
Table~\ref{tab:corpora} compares the seven corpora I considered. WikiText-2 is a standard language-modelling benchmark, but it is Wikipedia text, which GloVe was trained on, so Part~II's public vectors would have seen it. IMDB has sentiment labels and little overlap with GloVe, but its 50,000 unlabelled reviews, the natural language-model training text, are not documented as disjoint by movie from its labelled test set \citep{maas2011learning}. Amazon Movies \& TV has the same properties as All\_Beauty with about 25 times as many reviews; as the assignment allows, I took the category whose size suits one laptop.

\paragraph{Cleaning.}
Before tokenizing, Amazon video tags (in 5,951 reviews) become spaces, links to other products keep the product name (474 reviews), e-mail addresses are removed as personal data (42 reviews), ``\&'' becomes ``and'' and curly apostrophes are straightened. The course tokenizer is the regular expression \texttt{[a-z]+(?:'[a-z]+)?|[.,!?;:]} on lowercased text, extended to keep \tok{num} whole.

\paragraph{Lengths.}
Reviews under three words are 7.2\% of reviews but hold 0.4\% of tokens, and a minimum length would change the label mix (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}a), so they stay. The 512-token limit removes 723 reviews (0.10\%) and lets one Transformer context of 513 positions hold every review with its \tok{bos}.

\paragraph{English only.}
fastText's language identifier \citep{joulin2017bag,joulin2016fasttextzip}, its compressed lid.176 model used through the fast-langdetect package, would on its own remove 15,434 reviews, a third of them of one or two words, where its guesses are least reliable: of 25 one- or two-word reviews it labelled non-English with probability below 0.5, only 11 were foreign. Curly apostrophes also made it label English reviews as Russian or Thai, so they are straightened first. My word score sums, over a review's words, the log of how much more often each word appears in non-English than in English reviews (a score of 2 means about 7 times). It is learnt from reviews of seven or more words that fastText labels with probability 0.9 or more (516,880 English, 5,090 other), so it inherits fastText's labels. Reviews of up to six words are removed when their score is 2 or more. Longer reviews are removed when fastText's top language is not English and either it is at least 90\% sure or the score is 2 or more, and also when a sentence of five or more words is non-English for fastText (probability 0.9 or more) with an average word score of 2 or more, as in an English review followed by a translation. The rule keeps 3,997 reviews that fastText flagged, almost all of them short (Table~\ref{tab:language}). Filtering a language-model corpus by language and duplicates follows C4 \citep{raffel2020exploring}.

\paragraph{Duplicates.}
Exact copies by the same person are one review counted again (8,021 removed), and near copies by the same person share 90\% or more of their distinct words (69 removed). A first line of 7 words for exact copies by different people removed mostly everyday sentences (8 of 10 in a hand-checked sample), so it moved to 14: on the final corpus, near-identical but not identical reviews by different people occur at every length from 7 to 13 words and never from 14 to 26 (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}b). Exact copies of 14 or more words by different people are removed (119).

\paragraph{Cap per product.}
In the raw data, the top 1\% of products held 28\% of reviews and one product had 1,962. Star ratings of one product correlate, with intraclass correlation $\rho = 0.1745$. By Kish's design effect, $m$ reviews of a product estimate its mean rating as precisely as $m/(1+(m-1)\rho)$ independent reviews would, which approaches $1/\rho = 5.73$; 90 is the smallest $m$ that reaches 95\% of that limit. Re-estimated on 50 random halves of the products, $\rho$ ranges from 0.170 to 0.181 and the cap from 87 to 93 (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}c). Kept reviews are chosen by a fixed random number per review (seed 4213).

\paragraph{Pile sizes.}
Pile sizes come from 20 slices of 5\% of the split keys. On every slice a unigram model's $J$ has a standard error of 0.0030 to 0.0035 nats when reviews are resampled, so 5\% is enough for validation and for test; this ignores the correlation between reviews of one product and the variation between training seeds. Training must cover $[0, 0.5)$ because the pilot run used products from that range. Larger training piles would lower every model's $J$ somewhat but shrink Part~III's balanced training set from 74,344 reviews to about 49,700 (training on $[0, 0.6)$, Part~III training on $[0.7, 0.9)$) or 24,700 (training on $[0, 0.7)$, Part~III training on $[0.9, 1)$); how the ranking changes with more training data is not tested.

\paragraph{Vocabulary.}
The cut-off was measured by building a vocabulary on the products with keys below 0.5, which later became the training pile, and counting \tok{unk} on the other half; swapping the halves gives the same curve (Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing}d). Lowering the minimum count from 10 to 5 adds 4,918 words and removes 0.28 percentage points of \tok{unk}; lowering it further to 3, 2 and 1 adds 5,279, 6,278 and 23,618 words for 0.15, 0.09 and 0.11 points. Five is also gensim word2vec's default minimum count \citep{rehurek2010software}, so Part~II's own embeddings see every vocabulary word at least five times.

\paragraph{Hand checks.}
I read random samples of each rule's decisions (seed 4213) and counted those the rule got right (Table~\ref{tab:handchecks}). Claude, the AI assistant used in this project (Appendix~\ref{app:repro}), counted the same samples. The counts agree on 7 of 8 samples. For samples 1 to 6 I had seen Claude's counts before counting; for 7 and 8 I counted first. The one disagreement is a review whose only non-English words are a five-word holiday greeting: I counted it as containing a foreign sentence, Claude did not. Samples of 10 are small: 10 of 10 right still allows an error rate of up to 26\% (one-sided 95\% bound).

\paragraph{Checks on the final corpus.}
A script reruns these checks on the file the models read (Table~\ref{tab:checks}). The corpus fingerprint (SHA-256 of the uncompressed file) starts \texttt{16ec4ec1}, so anyone who rebuilds the corpus can confirm it is identical.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Each limitation of the preprocessing is measured (Table~\ref{tab:limits}). Every filter was designed on the whole corpus before the split, and none used a model result, but some used text or ratings of products that later became evaluation products: the length rule compared the label mix of all reviews, the word score was learnt from all reviews, the cap's $\rho$ uses every product's ratings, and the vocabulary cut-off was compared on the other half of the products. These choices barely depend on which products became test products: the cap moves only between 87 and 93 across random halves of the products, and swapping the vocabulary halves gives the same curve.

\section{Model and Training Evidence}
\label{app:training}

S models are the main size; M models are the size check, with cores matched within 6.6\%.}

\end{table*}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{batch_size.pdf}
\caption{Pilot-run speed and memory by batch size. (a)~Training speed of the six candidate models; solid lines are the main size (S), dashed lines the size check (M). (b)~Peak memory over the six models: the band is their range and the line the largest. I use 8K positions per batch: speed rises up to 8K for every model and is flat or lower at 16K for five of six, and 8K stays below every step-300 estimate of the gradient noise scale.}
\label{fig:batch}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Pilot run.}
Before the real runs, a 28-minute pilot run trained each candidate model for 300 steps (about 0.2 epochs) at 8,192 positions per batch and a peak learning rate of $10^{-3}$, on products with keys below 0.45 and with its own vocabulary ($|V| = 16{,}270$); it validated on keys 0.45 to 0.5. It timed 10 steps at five batch sizes, logged unclipped gradient norms, and estimated the gradient noise scale $B_{\text{simple}}$ after 50, 150 and 300 steps from 8 micro-batches \citep[App.~A.1]{mccandlish2018empirical}. It set three values (Table~\ref{tab:pilot}, Figure~\ref{fig:batch}).
\emph{Batch size:} speed rises up to 8K positions for every model and is flat or lower at 16K for five of six (RNN-M gains 9\%); at 32K, memory reaches 11.1 to 14.1~GiB of 16~GiB and speed collapses. At step 300, $B_{\text{simple}}$ is at least 8,060 targets for every model, while an 8K batch holds about 7,150 targets and a 16K batch about 14,000, so 8K is the largest size below every step-300 estimate. The estimates are noisy: at step 150, RNN-M's was 5,977, and LSTM-S's was undefined because its estimate of the squared gradient norm $|G|^2$ came out negative. The throughput plateau therefore decides, and the noise scale only supports it.
\emph{Clipping:} 1.0 lies within half to ten times every model's mean gradient norm over the second half of the run, 0.67 to 1.21 \citep{pascanu2013difficulty}. The vanilla RNNs clip most often (23\% and 41\% of late steps) because their typical norm is near 1.0 (late means 0.96 and 1.21). Adam scales each step by a running average of gradient size, so I expect clipping to change little beyond trimming the largest steps; this is not tested.
\emph{Validation cost:} one validation pass took 8 to 10\,s. Evaluation time, including the training sample scored at each check, is logged separately and left out of training time.

\paragraph{$n$-gram models.}
Kneser-Ney uses the closed-form discounts of \citet[eq.~26]{chen1998empirical} for counts of 1, 2, and 3 or more, with continuation counts for the lower orders; $n$-grams that start with \tok{bos} keep their raw counts, as in \citet[3.2]{heafield2013scalable}, because no word can come before \tok{bos}; a discount outside its valid range falls back to 0.5, 1 or 1.5, as in KenLM's discount fallback. Add-$k$ interpolates add-$k$ estimates of every order up to $n$. Its $k$ is searched over powers of ten from $10^{-4}$ to 1, and the grid is extended tenfold while the best value is at an edge; its weights are fit by EM on validation data \citep{jurafsky2026speech}, so its validation $J$ is slightly optimistic, but its test $J$ is not. Both choose $n = 5$ on validation, where Kneser-Ney beats order 4 by only 0.003 nats, because 79\% of validation 5-grams never occur in training. I did not use KenLM, which rejects \tok{unk} in its input. Tests check that every distribution sums to 1 and that my Kneser-Ney matches a slow reference implementation for orders 1 to 4.

\paragraph{Recipe and sources.}
Table~\ref{tab:recipe} lists every setting with its evidence. The pilot run checked three of them on this data (batch size, clipping and validation cost); the others follow the cited sources, most of which study larger Transformer models with subword tokens.

\paragraph{Rules fixed before any result.}
\label{app:rules}
Three rules were written down before the first run, so the results cannot steer them.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item \emph{Overfitting.} A model overfits if its validation $J$ stops improving while its training-sample $J$ keeps falling, before the last quarter of its planned run. If any model does, all three get a run with dropout 0.1 on the input embeddings and before the output layer, at their chosen learning rates; if that lowers any model's validation $J$, all three get one more run at 0.3. Main results stay at dropout 0. \emph{Outcome:} no run met the rule (every kept 6-epoch run's best checkpoint is one of its last two checks), so no dropout runs were made.
\item \emph{Training budget.} If a model's validation $J$ still falls in its last epoch by more than the gap to its neighbour in the ranking, all three models get one longer run (10 epochs) at their chosen rates, and both budgets are reported. \emph{Outcome:} the LSTM's validation $J$ fell by 0.023 in its last epoch against a gap of 0.010 to the Transformer, so all three got 10-epoch runs (Table~\ref{tab:part1}).
\item \emph{Short tries.} The validation checks show which rate one-epoch tries would have chosen, and whether it matches the full-run winner. Short tries can mislead either way: short horizons favour small step sizes \citep{wu2018understanding}, while the best learning rate falls as training gets longer \citep{bjorck2025scaling}. \emph{Outcome:} validation $J$ after one epoch picks the same rate as the full tries for all six models.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Change after the first results.}
The tuning rule fixed before the runs allowed one step past an edge. The LSTM's best rate was then the largest it tried (0.01, after 0.0003, 0.001 and 0.003), so before the Transformer's and RNN's tries finished, I extended the rule for every model: keep stepping half a decade outward while the best rate stays at the edge, as \citet[3.3.1]{bengio2012practical} recommends. The extension tried 0.03 for the LSTM-S and LSTM-M, which was worse in both cases, so 0.01 stayed; every other model's best rate was already inside its tries (Table~\ref{tab:tuning}).

\paragraph{Limitations of the recipe.}
The shared settings may suit one model better than another, since only the learning rate is tuned per model. A few tries find a good learning rate, not always the best, and the winner can depend on the tuning budget \citep{dodge2019show}, so I report the tries. AdamW may slightly hold back the RNN and LSTM: plain SGD has been reported to work better for LSTM language models \citep{merity2018regularizing}, though that paper does not test Adam itself. The 100 numbers that feed each output layer limit the rank of every model's score matrix \citep{yang2018breaking}, equally for all three, which may shrink the gaps between them; tying $E$ to the output layer would improve perplexity \citep{press2017using} but would freeze the output layer with $E$ in Part~II.

\section{Additional Part II Details}
\label{app:part2}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\input{tables/part2_words.tex}
\caption{The two pretrained tables on the course's word tests, on the 16,544 vocabulary words both have, and their nearest neighbours (cosine).}
\label{tab:part2-words}
\end{table*}

\paragraph{Coverage and missing words.}
Of the 17,064 vocabulary words, 16,256 (95.3\%) have an exact GloVe vector, 279 contractions are built from their halves (GloVe's tokenizer splits ``don't'' into ``do'' and ``n't''), and 9 words that CoreNLP splits, such as ``cannot'' and ``gonna'', from their pieces; \tok{num} takes the average of GloVe's number vectors among its 10,000 most frequent words. The other 522 rows, 519 rare words such as ``reccomend'' and ``polygel'' plus \tok{bos}, \tok{unk} and \tok{eos}, are random with the mean square of GloVe's exact rows \citep{kim2014convolutional}; \tok{pad} is zero. The frozen random table has the same root mean square (0.541), about nine times the trainable table's starting scale (0.058), so the 0.319-nat cost of freezing it mixes the loss of trainability with a change of scale. My skip-gram table (gensim, window 5, 5 negative samples, 15 epochs, $d = 100$, one thread, seed 4213) is multiplied by 1.69 so its root mean square matches GloVe's (0.541).

\paragraph{Learning-rate check.}
At seed 4213 the fixed tables were also trained at 0.003, 0.03 and 0.1. My vectors reach validation $J$ 3.965, 3.815, 3.800 and 4.532 at 0.003, 0.01, 0.03 and 0.1, GloVe 4.099, 3.976, 3.919 and 4.805; both 0.1 runs were unstable and stopped early. The trainable random table is best at 0.01 (0.03: 3.726). The order of the settings is the same at each setting's best rate, and the main comparison stays at 0.01, as fixed before the runs.

\paragraph{Test $J$ per seed.}
For seeds 4213, 4214 and 4215, the random trainable table reaches 3.708, 3.703 and 3.704, my frozen vectors 3.811, 3.795 and 3.810, and frozen GloVe 3.973, 3.959 and 3.954. Freezing therefore costs 0.103, 0.091 and 0.107 nats with my vectors and 0.265, 0.256 and 0.250 with GloVe: the order is the same on every seed.

\paragraph{Stability and tables.}
Gradient norms are similar in every setting (mean 0.30 to 0.40); the input table's own gradient is small (mean norm 0.025 against 0.30 for all parameters). Every fixed table's fingerprint is identical before and after training. The trainable random table's root mean square grew from 0.058 to 0.657 (median cosine between a row's start and end 0.06); trainable GloVe moved less (median cosine 0.55). The \texttt{gensim} log reports 309 ignored exceptions: its compiled code mistakes a dot product of exactly $-1.0$ for an error code and uses 0 in that one update, 309 times in roughly ten billion, so I ignore them.

\label{tab:part3}

\paragraph{Protocol.}
Features are read in evaluation mode with the model's parameters checked unchanged by fingerprint; feature extraction for the whole test set took 1.0 to 2.8 seconds per model on the GPU. Before the test set was touched, every checkpoint's validation $J$ was recomputed and matched its record within $10^{-4}$, and an untrained copy built twice gave identical weights. $C$ is searched over $10^{-4}$ to $10^{2}$; if the best value is uniquely at the top it grows tenfold (limit $10^{6}$), it shrinks only when the lowest value strictly beats all others (limit $10^{-8}$), and ties go to the smaller $C$. Folds are stratified by label and grouped by product (seed 4213), identical for every representation, and no product is on both sides of a fold. Word counts keep word and word-pair columns seen in at least two fitting reviews, weighted by tf-idf on each fitting part only. Bootstrap intervals use 2,000 resamples of test reviews shared by every representation; a second set resamples whole products, because reviews of one product are not independent.

\paragraph{Copies between piles.}
Products never cross piles, but short everyday reviews recur across people (kept by design, Appendix~\ref{app:data}): 6.4\% of test texts also appear in the language-model training pile and 5.1\% in Part~III's training set, mostly reviews of one or two words (69\% of which repeat a Part~III training review). A pure lookup of repeated texts would be right on 98.5\% of them; the main model scores 98.4\% on them against 93.0\% on new text. Without reviews under 3 or 5 words, $\tau$ is unchanged for the last word (0.69) and 0.87 and 0.86 for the average.

\paragraph{Top hidden state.}
As a check on the readout, I also classified the top hidden state of the six Part~I models (100 to 1,120 numbers; Table~\ref{tab:part3-all}). It gives close results, for example 93.6\% for Transformer-M and 93.7\% for LSTM-M at the last word, and RNN-S still loses 5.5 points at its last word (85.1\% against 90.6\% averaged).

\paragraph{Checks added while writing.}
Table~\ref{tab:exploratory} was not fixed in advance and is exploratory. With averaged features, every pair of models at least 0.05 nats apart in test $J$ is in the same order. Without the three RNNs, $\tau$ is 0.69 for the last word and 0.78 for the average. Against word counts, uncorrected McNemar tests give $p = 0.29$ (LSTM-M) and 0.07 (Transformer-M) at the last word, and 0.50 and 0.88 for their top hidden states.

\paragraph{Error categories.}
Table~\ref{tab:error-categories} gives the counts. The list was fixed before any mistake was read: rating does not match the text; mixed feelings; negation missed; sarcasm; complaint not about the product; too short or vague; other; the first that applies wins. Claude drafted a category and a one-line reason for each of the 40 sampled mistakes; I read every review and decided each category. After that first reading I revised the list, so the final categories are not the ones fixed in advance: ``mixed'' now requires real good and bad points of the product as it is now (a review that calls one side the only good or bad thing, such as ``the only plus'' or ``only complaint'', or praises an older version, belongs to its overall side); the catch-all ``other'' held reviews any reader can label at once, so it was split by overall side into ``negative, but told as plain facts'', ``negative, but with some praise'' and ``positive overall''; ``negation missed'' was dropped (its positive reviews that praise through ``not'' moved to ``positive overall'', and its one negative warning to ``negative, but told as plain facts''); and ``rating does not match'' became ``stars do not match the text''. The 5 plus 5 random disagreements between the main model and word counts follow the same pattern as the examples in Section~\ref{sec:part3}.

\section{Reproducibility, Data and AI Use}
\label{app:repro}

\paragraph{Code and reproducibility.}
The repository (\url{https://github.com/kr7001/dsa4213-assignment}) holds every script, configuration and result file behind this report; its README lists the data download, every command in order, the configurations and the seeds (4213 throughout, plus 4214 and 4215 for Part~II's repeats). It uses Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.14.1 \citep{paszke2019pytorch}, gensim 4.4.0 \citep{rehurek2010software} and scikit-learn 1.9.1 \citep{pedregosa2011scikit}, with every dependency pinned in \texttt{uv.lock}. Every run records its git commit, whether the code had uncommitted changes, its configuration, device and machine; the test suite (168 tests) passes. Every table and figure of results is written by \texttt{scripts/make\_report\_figures.py} from the result files, and \texttt{scripts/check\_report\_numbers.py} checks the numbers in this text against them.

\paragraph{Data.}
Amazon Reviews 2023 states no licence, so the repository holds only the download script, never the data, and I cite the dataset \citep{hou2024bridging}; generated samples and review text stay on my machine, apart from the short quotes and samples shown in this report. GloVe is released under the Open Data Commons Public Domain Dedication and License, and the fastText language-identification model under CC BY-SA 3.0.

\paragraph{AI use.}
I used Claude (Anthropic) throughout, as the brief allows. Claude helped to research different options for the decisions, wrote the code to my design (data pipeline, models, tests and figure scripts), suggested a category for each of the 40 sampled errors, and drafted the report text. I made every design and architecture decision, ran every experiment on my own machine and reviewed its results, decided every error category myself, and revised the report drafts in my own words, style and format. I checked Claude's suggestions against the results and my own reading, and changed them where they did not make sense to me (for example, I revised the error categories).
